column3: Therefore Festus, having entered the province, after three days went up from Caesarea to Jerusalem.
And the chief priests and the leading men of the Jews presented charges against Paul, and they were urging Festus,
asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, while they were preparing an ambush to kill him along the road.
Festus therefore answered that Paul was being kept in Caesarea and that he himself was about to go there shortly.
“So,” he said, “let the powerful men among you come down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”
After staying among them no more than eight or ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat and commanded Paul to be brought.
When he arrived, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing many serious charges that they were unable to prove.
Paul defended himself: “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar have I sinned in anything.”
But Festus, wanting to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged there before me concerning these things?”
But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be judged. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well.

If then I am doing wrong and have done anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is nothing to the things of which these men accuse me, no one can hand me over to them as a favor. I appeal to Caesar.”
Then Festus, after conferring with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar; to Caesar you will go.”
Now after some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived in Caesarea and greeted Festus.
And as they were spending several days there, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left behind as a prisoner by Felix,
about whom, when I was in Jerusalem, the chief priests and elders of the Jews presented charges, asking for a sentence against him.
I answered them that it is not the custom of Romans to hand over any man before the accused has his accusers face to face and receives an opportunity for defense concerning the charge.
Therefore when they came together here, I made no delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat and commanded the man to be brought.
When the accusers stood around him, they brought no charge concerning the evil things I was expecting,
but they had certain disputes with him about their own religion and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul kept affirming to be alive.
And being perplexed about the investigation of these things, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and be judged there concerning these matters.
But when Paul appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I send him to Caesar.”
Agrippa said to Festus, “I myself also would like to hear the man.” He said, “Tomorrow you will hear him.”

Therefore on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice came with great display and entered the audience hall together with commanders and prominent men of the city, at the command of Festus Paul was brought in.

And Festus said, “King Agrippa and all men present with us, you see this man about whom the whole multitude of the Jews appealed to me, both in Jerusalem and here, crying out that he ought not to live any longer.
But I found that he had done nothing worthy of death, and since he himself appealed to the emperor, I decided to send him.

Concerning him I have nothing certain to write to my lord. Therefore I brought him before you all, and especially before you, King Agrippa, so that after the examination I may have something to write.
For it seems unreasonable to me, when sending a prisoner, not also to indicate the charges against him.”
